audio/welcome.mp3: Start here. Ten short lessons on how the world moves, with no equations. Every picture below the title is alive: drag it, tap it, change it, and watch what happens. Then answer one question to mark the lesson done.
audio/nope.mp3: Not quite. Try the sim again, then pick another answer.
audio/motion-hero.mp3: Things keep going. A moving thing does not stop on its own. Something has to slow it down.
audio/motion-try.mp3: Try this. Flick the ball on ice, then on carpet. Where does it travel farther? Switch to Space and flick. Wait for it to stop. (Keep waiting.). Flick gently, then hard. Does a harder flick change how the ball slows, or only how far it goes?
audio/motion-saw.mp3: What you saw. The ball never "ran out of push." The floor rubbed on it and stole its motion a little at a time. Rough floors steal faster. In space there is nothing to rub, so it rolls forever. Scientists call the rubbing friction, and the keep-going-ness inertia.
audio/motion-quiz.mp3: Quick check. A hockey puck slides across the ice and slowly comes to a stop. Why? First answer: It ran out of push. Second answer: The ice rubs on it a tiny bit, and that rubbing slows it. Third answer: Pucks always stop after a few seconds no matter what.
audio/motion-why.mp3: Yes. Even ice has a little grip. Less grip than carpet, so the puck goes far, but not forever.
audio/forces-hero.mp3: Pushes and pulls. When pushes are equal, nothing moves. When one side pushes harder, things move that way.
audio/forces-try.mp3: Try this. Give both teams the same number of pullers. Watch the rope. Add one more puller to a side. Which way does the knot move? Make it four against one. Does the knot move faster than three against two?
audio/forces-saw.mp3: What you saw. Every pull is a force. Forces on opposite sides cancel each other out. Only the leftover pull moves the rope, and a bigger leftover moves it faster. A still rope does not mean nobody is pulling; it means the pulls are balanced.
audio/forces-quiz.mp3: Quick check. Both teams pull exactly as hard as each other. What does the rope do? First answer: Creeps toward the bigger-looking team. Second answer: Stays put, even though everyone is pulling. Third answer: Snaps.
audio/forces-why.mp3: Yes. Equal pulls cancel. The rope is under strain but it does not move. That is a balanced force.
audio/gravity-hero.mp3: Everything falls together. Without air in the way, a feather and a hammer fall side by side.
audio/gravity-try.mp3: Try this. Drop them on Earth with air. The feather floats down slowly. Turn the air off and drop again. Go to the Moon. There is no air there. Then watch the feather.
audio/gravity-saw.mp3: What you saw. Gravity pulls on everything the same way, so everything speeds up at the same rate as it falls. The feather only looks slow on Earth because air pushes back on it. Take the air away and the race is a tie. Astronaut Dave Scott did this for real on the Moon in 1971.
audio/gravity-quiz.mp3: Quick check. On the Moon, you drop a hammer and a feather at the same moment. Which lands first? First answer: The hammer, because it is heavier. Second answer: The feather, because it is lighter. Third answer: They land at the same time.
audio/gravity-why.mp3: Yes. No air on the Moon means nothing holds the feather back. Gravity treats both the same.
audio/energy-hero.mp3: Hills and swings. Height turns into speed, and speed turns back into height. Nothing is lost unless something rubs.
audio/energy-try.mp3: Try this. Drag the ball partway up the first hill and let go. See how high it climbs the next hill. Drag it to the very top. Can it clear the far hill now? Switch the track to Sticky. Where does the ball end up?
audio/energy-saw.mp3: What you saw. A ball up high is storing something: the ability to move. Rolling down cashes that in for speed. Rolling up spends speed to buy height again. With a smooth track the ball always climbs back to its starting height and never higher. A sticky track leaks that stored motion into heat, so each climb is a little lower.
audio/energy-quiz.mp3: Quick check. On a perfectly smooth track, you let a ball go from partway up a hill. How high does it climb the next hill? First answer: Higher than where it started. Second answer: Up to the same height it started from, never higher. Third answer: It stops at the bottom.
audio/energy-why.mp3: Yes. What it had in height becomes speed, then becomes height again. Same amount, same height.
audio/collisions-hero.mp3: Bump! When things crash, the heavier one mostly keeps going and the lighter one gets shoved.
audio/collisions-try.mp3: Try this. Launch a big ball into a small one. Watch the big one. Launch a small ball into a big one. Where does the small ball go? Make them the same size. What happens to the first ball? Turn on Sticky and try again.
audio/collisions-saw.mp3: What you saw. Motion gets passed along in a crash, but it is shared out by weight. A heavy thing carries lots of motion and barely notices a light thing. A light thing hitting a heavy thing bounces back. Two equal things swap: one stops dead, the other takes off with its motion. Sticky crashes keep both moving together, slower.
audio/collisions-quiz.mp3: Quick check. A bowling ball rolls into a single marble. What happens to the bowling ball? First answer: It stops dead. Second answer: It bounces straight back. Third answer: It barely slows down.
audio/collisions-why.mp3: Yes. The marble is too light to take much motion away. The bowling ball keeps nearly all of it.
audio/heat-hero.mp3: Hot is jiggly. Hot means the tiny pieces inside are jiggling fast. Cold means they jiggle slowly.
audio/heat-try.mp3: Try this. Turn the left cup all the way cold. Watch the dots lock into place. Turn it all the way hot. The dots break loose and fly. Set one cup hot and one cold, then open the wall between them. Watch what happens to both.
audio/heat-saw.mp3: What you saw. Everything is made of tiny pieces that never sit still. More jiggle is what we feel as heat. Slow jiggle lets the pieces hold hands in a pattern: that is a solid. Faster, they slide past each other: a liquid. Faster still, they fly apart: a gas. When hot touches cold, the fast ones bump the slow ones until everybody jiggles about the same. Heat always flows from hot to cold, never the other way by itself.
audio/heat-quiz.mp3: Quick check. A hot cup and a cold cup sit touching each other. After a while, what do you find? First answer: The hot one got hotter. Second answer: Both ended up in between, the same as each other. Third answer: Nothing changes until you stir.
audio/heat-why.mp3: Yes. Jiggle spreads out by bumping. It evens out, and it never piles up on one side by itself.
audio/sound-hero.mp3: Wiggles you can hear. Sound is something wiggling back and forth, shaking the air all the way to your ear.
audio/sound-try.mp3: Try this. Pull the string down and let go. Turn your sound on first. Tighten the string and pluck again. Higher or lower? Pluck gently, then pluck hard. What changes, and what stays the same?
audio/sound-saw.mp3: What you saw. A plucked string wiggles, and each wiggle gives the air next to it a shove. Those shoves travel outward as ripples. A tight string wiggles faster, and faster wiggles sound higher. A bigger wiggle shoves harder and sounds louder, but it does not change the note. Pitch comes from how fast, loudness from how big.
audio/sound-quiz.mp3: Quick check. You want a higher note from a string. What do you do? First answer: Tighten the string so it wiggles faster. Second answer: Pluck it harder. Third answer: Loosen the string.
audio/sound-why.mp3: Yes. Tighter means faster wiggles. Faster wiggles are what we hear as a higher pitch. Plucking harder only makes it louder.
audio/light-hero.mp3: Light goes straight. Light travels in straight lines, so anything in the way leaves a dark patch behind it.
audio/light-try.mp3: Try this. Drag the lamp close to the toy. What happens to the shadow on the wall? Drag the lamp far away. Now? Turn on the second lamp. Count the shadows and look at where they overlap.
audio/light-saw.mp3: What you saw. Light leaves the lamp in every direction and keeps going straight. The toy blocks some of it, and the blocked lines mark out a shadow. Close to the lamp the toy blocks a wide fan of lines, so the shadow is huge. Two lamps make two shadows, and only where both are blocked is it fully dark.
audio/light-quiz.mp3: Quick check. You move the lamp closer to the toy. The shadow on the wall gets... First answer: Bigger. Second answer: Smaller. Third answer: It stays the same size.
audio/light-why.mp3: Yes. Up close, the toy blocks a wider slice of the light fanning out from the lamp. The shadow spreads.
audio/magnets-hero.mp3: Push and pull without touching. Magnets reach through empty space. Matching ends push apart, opposite ends pull together.
audio/magnets-try.mp3: Try this. Drag the blue-and-red magnet toward the other one. Watch it react before they touch. Tap Flip to turn the loose magnet around, then come close again. Turn on the filings to see the invisible pattern around them.
audio/magnets-saw.mp3: What you saw. A magnet has two ends, called north and south. North pulls south and pushes north. The pull or push works from a distance, and it gets stronger fast as the magnets get close. The pattern the filings make is the shape of that invisible reach. A compass is just a tiny magnet turning to line up with the Earth, which is a giant one.
audio/magnets-quiz.mp3: Quick check. You bring two north ends toward each other. They... First answer: Pull together. Second answer: Push apart. Third answer: Do nothing until they touch.
audio/magnets-why.mp3: Yes. Same ends push. Opposite ends pull. And it all happens before anything touches.
audio/floating-hero.mp3: Why boats float. Things float when they are less packed-in than water, and sink when they are more packed-in.
audio/floating-try.mp3: Try this. Drop a wooden block and a stone. Which goes down? Drop the egg. Now add salt to the water with the slider. Drop the ice cube. How much of it pokes out of the water?
audio/floating-saw.mp3: What you saw. Water pushes up on anything you put in it. If the thing is less tightly packed than water (a duck, wood, ice), that upward push wins and it floats. Packed tighter than water (stone, metal) and it sinks. Size does not matter: a giant log floats and a tiny key sinks. Salt packs the water tighter, which is why an egg floats in salty water and why it is easy to float in the sea.
audio/floating-quiz.mp3: Quick check. A huge wooden log floats but a tiny metal key sinks. Why? First answer: Big things float, small things sink. Second answer: It depends how tightly packed the stuff is compared to water, not how big it is. Third answer: Wood is lighter than water in total.
audio/floating-why.mp3: Yes. A log weighs far more than a key, yet it floats. What matters is packing, not size or total weight.
audio2/welcome.mp3: Level 2. Measure it. Level 1 was about feeling how things move. Now we write it down. Every lesson here has a measuring tool, a table of what you measured, and a graph that draws itself as you go. Still no equations. The graphs do the talking.
audio2/nope.mp3: Not quite. Measure again, then pick another answer.
audio2/ruler-hero.mp3: Ruler and stopwatch. Measure where something is and when it was there. Put the dots on a graph and a story appears.
audio2/ruler-try.mp3: Try this. Tap Start, then tap Lap every time the train passes a metre mark. Watch the dots land on the graph. Reset and try the fast train. Are the dots steeper or flatter? Turn on auto-lap and compare the three speeds.
audio2/ruler-saw.mp3: What you saw. Each lap is one measurement: a time and a place. On the graph, a steady train makes dots that line up in a straight slope. A faster train makes a steeper slope, because it covers more metres in each second. The slope of a position time graph is the speed, and you can read it without any formula: look at how many metres it climbs per second.
audio2/ruler-quiz.mp3: Quick check. A train at steady speed makes a position time graph that is... First answer: A straight sloping line. Second answer: A curve that bends upward. Third answer: A flat line.
audio2/ruler-why.mp3: Yes. Same metres every second means the dots climb by the same amount each second, which is a straight line.
audio2/match-hero.mp3: Match the graph. A position time graph is a recording of a walk. You can read a walk off it, and you can walk one into it.
audio2/match-try.mp3: Try this. Tap Start and drag the walker so your line lands on the target line. Find the flat part. What do you have to do to make a flat line? Try the other two targets. One of them has you walking back.
audio2/match-saw.mp3: What you saw. Flat means standing still. Sloping up means walking away from the start. Sloping down means walking back. Steeper means faster. Once you can feel that in your thumb, you can read any position time graph like a sentence.
audio2/match-quiz.mp3: Quick check. A flat part of a position time graph means the walker is... First answer: Standing still. Second answer: Walking at a steady speed. Third answer: Speeding up.
audio2/match-why.mp3: Yes. Flat means the position is not changing as time goes by, so the walker is not moving.
audio2/speed-hero.mp3: Speed up, slow down. A speed time graph shows how fast, not where. The space under the line is how far you went.
audio2/speed-try.mp3: Try this. Hold Gas for a few seconds, let go, then hold Brake. Watch the line rise, level out, and fall. Drive at a steady speed. What shape does the line make? Compare the shaded area with the distance readout.
audio2/speed-saw.mp3: What you saw. On this graph, up and down means faster and slower, not forward and back. Gas makes the line climb. Brake makes it drop. Letting go makes it drift down a little, because the road rubs. The shaded area under the line grows exactly as fast as the odometer, because distance is speed stacked up over time.
audio2/speed-quiz.mp3: Quick check. A speed time line sloping downward means the car is... First answer: Slowing down. Second answer: Going backwards. Third answer: Stopped.
audio2/speed-why.mp3: Yes. The height of the line is the speed. Going down means less speed, which is slowing. Direction is not on this graph at all.
audio2/drop-hero.mp3: Dropping and timing. A falling ball speeds up as it goes. Measuring the drop shows the shape of that speeding up.
audio2/drop-try.mp3: Try this. Drop from 1 metre, then 2 metres, then 4 metres. Compare the times in the table. Switch the graph to speed and drop again. What shape is the line? Turn on slow motion to watch the ball speed up.
audio2/drop-saw.mp3: What you saw. Four times the height does not take four times as long. It takes about twice as long. That is because the ball is not moving at one speed: it starts slow and gets faster every moment. The speed time graph says the same thing more simply: a straight rising line, which means the speed grows by the same amount every second.
audio2/drop-quiz.mp3: Quick check. Dropping a ball from 4 metres instead of 1 metre takes... First answer: About twice as long. Second answer: Four times as long. Third answer: The same time.
audio2/drop-why.mp3: Yes. Because the ball keeps speeding up, the lower metres go by faster than the first one.
audio2/spring-hero.mp3: Stretch a spring. Add weight, measure the stretch. The graph tells you when a spring is behaving and when it is ruined.
audio2/spring-try.mp3: Try this. Add 100 grams at a time and read the ruler. How much extra stretch does each 100 grams give? Keep going past 600 grams, up to 800 grams. Watch the dots leave the straight line. Take all the weight off. Does the spring go back to where it started?
audio2/spring-saw.mp3: What you saw. For a while, every extra 100 grams stretches the spring by the same extra 2 centimetres. Same step, same stretch: the dots fall on a straight line. That is what makes a spring useful as a scale. Load it too much and the line bends: the metal is giving way, and when you unload it the spring stays longer than it was. Measuring is how you find that limit before you break something.
audio2/spring-quiz.mp3: Quick check. Each extra 100 grams stretched the spring by the same amount. On the graph that shows up as... First answer: A straight line. Second answer: A curve that gets steeper. Third answer: A flat line.
audio2/spring-why.mp3: Yes. Equal steps in weight giving equal steps in stretch is the definition of a straight line.
audio2/pendulum-hero.mp3: Swing timer. What decides how fast a pendulum swings? Measure it and find out which things do not matter.
audio2/pendulum-try.mp3: Try this. Time three swings at a short length, then a long length. Keep the length the same and switch the bob from light to heavy. Time it again. Try a small swing and a big swing. Compare.
audio2/pendulum-saw.mp3: What you saw. Only the length changes the time in a way you can see. Longer swings slower. The heavy bob and the light bob take the same time, and a small swing takes almost exactly as long as a big one. The dots make a curve that climbs quickly at first and then flattens: doubling the length does not double the time. Galileo noticed this with a swinging lamp in church and started timing it with his pulse.
audio2/pendulum-quiz.mp3: Quick check. Which change makes the biggest difference to how long a swing takes? First answer: Making the string longer. Second answer: Making the bob heavier. Third answer: Pulling it back further.
audio2/pendulum-why.mp3: Yes. Mass and swing size barely move the dots. Length moves them a lot.
audio2/heat-hero.mp3: Heat it up. Put a thermometer in melting ice and keep the burner on. The reading does something strange.
audio2/heat-try.mp3: Try this. Turn the burner on and watch the line. Where does it go flat? Switch the burner to high. Do the flat parts move up or down, or stay put? Let it boil. Does the water ever get hotter than 100?
audio2/heat-saw.mp3: What you saw. The thermometer climbs, then stops dead at 0 while the ice melts, even though heat is pouring in. Then it climbs again and stops at 100 while the water boils. During a flat part, all the heat is going into changing the state, solid to liquid or liquid to gas, not into warming anything. A stronger burner makes the climbs steeper and the flat parts shorter, but it never moves them: melting is 0 and boiling is 100, whatever you do.
audio2/heat-quiz.mp3: Quick check. While the ice is melting, the thermometer... First answer: Stays at 0 even though heat keeps going in. Second answer: Climbs steadily. Third answer: Drops a little.
audio2/heat-why.mp3: Yes. Melting takes heat without raising the temperature. The reading only moves again once all the ice is gone.
audio2/dunk-hero.mp3: Weigh it, dunk it. Two measurements, grams and millilitres, predict floating before you touch the water.
audio2/dunk-try.mp3: Try this. Measure the stone and the wood block. Look at where they land compared to the water line. Measure the egg and the plum. They are close to the line. Which side? Find a tiny thing that sinks and a big thing that floats.
audio2/dunk-saw.mp3: What you saw. Water weighs 1 gram for every millilitre, so the water line on the graph is the dividing line. Anything plotted above it packs more grams into its millilitres than water does, and sinks. Anything below floats. A big thing can be below the line and a tiny thing above it. The graph makes the rule visible: it is not weight alone and not size alone, but weight compared with size.
audio2/dunk-quiz.mp3: Quick check. An object plots above the water line, with more grams than millilitres. It will... First answer: Sink. Second answer: Float. Third answer: It depends how big it is.
audio2/dunk-why.mp3: Yes. Above the line means heavier than the same amount of water. The water cannot hold it up.
audio2/sound-hero.mp3: See the sound. An oscilloscope draws the wiggle. Count the wiggles in a slice of time and you have measured a note.
audio2/sound-try.mp3: Try this. Slide the pitch up. Do the wiggles get closer together or further apart? Slide the loudness. What changes and what stays the same? Read the wiggles-per-second number. Tap Play to hear that note.
audio2/sound-saw.mp3: What you saw. The screen shows how the air pushes on your ear, moment by moment. A higher note means more wiggles in the same slice of time, so they look squashed together. A louder note means taller wiggles, but the same spacing. Wiggles per second is the one number that names a note. Scientists call it hertz. The lowest note on a piano is about 27, the highest about 4,000.
audio2/sound-quiz.mp3: Quick check. A higher note shows up on the screen as... First answer: Wiggles packed closer together. Second answer: Taller wiggles. Third answer: A flatter line.
audio2/sound-why.mp3: Yes. Pitch is wiggles per second. More of them in the same time means they are closer together.
